And again, I'm not sure if it's before the Court or not in this respect, but at least one or two individuals from Pilica did go down to the headquarters of the Zvornik Brigade to complain about the circumstances and the crowding of prisoners in Pilica. And then further down on that page, the notation for Beara to call 155. And in this particular case, directly corresponds to one of our prior intercepts. I just want to highlight at this point, with respect to what I'm putting before the Court, I'm only highlighting those issues which I believe have some involvement with the criminal aspects that we see in the Zvornik Brigade. I'm not going through and trying to identify each and every line of the document where I can find a Zvornik Brigade notation in a document or an order or intercept with respect to legitimate combat activities or things of that nature. Some of those I will do because of their large scope and it's clearly evident, but I haven't gotten into the microanalysis to that level.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, if this is 14 July in the workbook, and if Mr. Jokic is the duty officer on 14 July, would it make sense that Jokic would write down his own name?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't speculate to that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, this reference to Beara to call 155, can you tie that into anything from any other information.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe, as I've just noted, going back to one of the prior intercept exhibits, referencing a conversation between Colonel Beara and Major Jokic, and I believe that's Prosecution Exhibit 232, there is a specific reference, and if I can put that back on the ELMO, to the issue of 155 called and asked you to call him urgently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's keep going.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- in this context, the last issues I'd like to highlight for the day of 14 July pertain another notation from Beara that Drago is to report and a notation that at 0900 hours, Beara is coming. I take that to mean that -- a notation that Beara is expected to be in the Zvornik Brigade headquarters by 9.00 the next morning, which will be the 15th. Certainly in context with the intercept that we've just discussed, Colonel Beara is not at the Zvornik Brigade headquarters at that time; he's at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How do you -- I'm sorry, I did not ask you that at that conversation, so could you put that intercept back on the screen and tell us why you conclude based on that intercept. Again, that's exhibit --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why you think Beara is where he is.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The notation in the text, "Hello Badem, let me talk to Beara." Badem is the telephonic code name for the headquarters of the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the last item on page 15 of the English language translation of the workbook reflects the report for the corps. And as you can see, that is almost the verbatim text of the 14 July interim combat report that is sent from the Zvornik Brigade to the command of the Drina Corps discussing the situation with the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: For the record, that interim report was 520. One other question, Mr. Butler, before you leave that on the "0900, Beara is coming." On the intercepts you've gone over already that involve Beara and Zivanovic and extension 139, does that help you in looking into the location of Beara and the meaning of this intercept?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I had made that analysis even for the Krstic case several years ago, that I believe that Colonel Beara was making the phone call to General Zivanovic and then later to General Krstic from the headquarters of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade. This piece of data just helps to lend more evidence to that analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's -- before we get into -- let's save the 15th in the book until we go through some of the documents for the 15th. So I believe we need to go back to 534, if I haven't confused the issue.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: 534 is another extract from a logbook which was turned over to the Office of the Prosecutor several months ago by Colonel Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What logbook, what's your understanding of what that logbook is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This I call the garrison duty officer logbook. There were two duty officers on duty that night or two duty positions with respect to function that are normally associated with the brigade. And both of these functions are again discussed in the 1983 JNA command and staff regulations. One, of course, is the duty operations officer, which you are familiar with. Another one is the duty officer or in this particular case the duty non-commissioned officer who was responsible for the issues pertaining to the physical facilities of the garrison. This is a particular one-page extract for the evening -- or for 14, 15 July, where the notations are -- the report of the situation in the barracks. And as you can tell, most of these notations here reflect the fact that the scope of duty of this particular individual and the scope of duty of the garrison duty officer is very much limited to barracks-related administrative. In this particular case, I'd just like to highlight the duty officer of the garrison noting that, through the evening of 14 and 15 July 1995, a bus with prisoners stayed overnight at the compound of the barracks, in standard facility proper. And it also notes that the body of troops at the barracks was not counted, due to the activities in the field, again everyone's deployed to the field to deal with issues related to the column as well as guarding prisoners of war, and this non-commissioned officer makes the observation that practically only the operations duty officer, the duty officer, and guards are located at the barracks at this point in time. Moving to page 7 of that English translation, the only other notation in this for the 15th and 16th that I would like to highlight is with respect to incoming reinforcements that begin arriving into the zone of the Zvornik Brigade by the morning of the 15th. And the second notation notes that a new shift from the Bratunac Brigade has arrived which was sent to the field some time later at approximately 1000 hours, that's noted. And it notes that at 1200 hours that elements of the Podrinje special forces detachment, which is the Drina Wolves a unit subordinate to the Zvornik Infantry Brigade are also starting to arrive back at the barracks location.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you know if Vinko Pandurevic was with them?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: While not noted in these particular documents, the commander of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade, Colonel Vinko Pandurevic, did come back with these units and is known to have arrived back at the headquarters of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade at approximately noon on 15 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the next document. I think we're going back to the engineering order of the day book, this time dated 15 July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, and it's Prosecution Exhibit 521.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: And this reflects the daily tasks of the engineering company. And looking at items 4 and 5, it reflects the work of an ULT-220 and a BGH-700 at Orahovac. And it reflects the work of an ULT and an excavator at Petkovci. Now, in context with the time we know from vehicle records that they are still continuing the burial of bodies at Orahovac on the morning and afternoon hours of 15 July 1995. And from our survivor accounts at Petkovci, the last of the executions at the dam occur at approximately 5.00 or 6.00 in the morning as the sun is starting to come up. And the burial activity there begins as the sun comes up. So I believe what you're looking at in notations 4 through 7 are the notations by the engineer company commander or the duty officer at the command at the time with respect to the burial of bodies from the executions at Orahovac and at the Petkovci or the dam.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you have any vehicle logs reflecting any work at Petkovci?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. None of the vehicle logs from the Zvornik Infantry Brigade indicate that their equipment was used at Petkovci dam during those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Number 1 says, "Pioneers to work in the area of Petkovci." What are pioneers again?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've noted in my earlier testimony, pioneers is the phrase or terminology referred to as combat engineers or is also known in another phrase as sappers. These are engineers strictly related to combat focuses, building small bunkers, laying mines, taking out mines, those direct small-level engineering functions to support combat commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And also it says power saw operators to work in the area of Petkovci. Besides the work that was going on at the dam regarding corpses on the 15th, are you aware of any pioneer work or chain saw work in the area of Petkovci village? Do you know what these might be referring to, 1 and 2?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indicated in the general context of the situation and in the brigade command's reports, the units that were considered most at risk for the enemy column going through the rear area were the 7th Infantry Battalion, the 4th Infantry Battalion and the 6th Infantry Battalion. The 6th Infantry battalion was the northern most of the three. And in this respect what I believe you're seeing is in notations 1 and 2, activity related to the very rapid construction of combat bunkers or fortifications in a very quick manner to try and deal with the column as it comes through the rear area of the 6th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So could these heavy excavators be used for this as well?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a possibility that was actively explored by myself and the investigation team, and the information we have available to us is that the battalion commanders and deputy command in question, when they discussed this issue with the OTP, did not note that they had requested this type of heavy equipment as part of their defensive operations. So again, that's one of the things that I used to conclude that items 6 and 7 are dealing with respect to the criminal acts and not the military ones. The second issue and where, perhaps, the map will make this more clear is that this red line depicting in rough terms the route of the column, where it would be penetrating the side of the 6th Battalion sector in Petkovci, yet survivor accounts indicate that construction equipment was used here at the dam at approximately -- starting at sun up on the morning of the 15th. So with respect to the overall military context of the situation, there wouldn't be any need to be conducting engineering activities at the foot of the dam at Petkovci, given the fact that the route of the column would not come anywhere near that location.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The village of Petkovci and the actual location of the dam are as depicted in this map. Do you know roughly how far Petkovci village and the dam are from each other?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure of the exact distance of the village per se, but I believe that we've calculated the distance from the old school at Petkovci which is the battalion headquarters of the 6th Battalion to the dam as approximately -- sorry. From the old school to the new school is approximately 800 metres and then further on to the dam is approximately 2 kilometres. I believe that's my recollection, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go on to the next exhibit. It looks like another vehicle log, 522.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is another piece of equipment noted owned by Birac Holding, as you can see on the English language translation, for an ULT-220 backhoe excavator. It notes 50 -- or 60 litres of fuel on 15 July, and it notes another 40 litres also on 15 July. And going to page 2 of the vehicle log, it reflects on 15 July, five hours of digging trenches at Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, is that consistent with the engineering logbook that we saw before?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is the name of the operator on this log?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name of the operator is on this log, however, that particular individual is not listed on the log of the engineering company, to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So what do you think that means?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just as the equipment may well have been requisitioned out of Birac Holding, I suspect the operator came with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, just for clarification, the description is backhoe excavator, as I think we've seen plenty of testimony, and ULT-220 is, in fact, a loader. So that's a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could go on to the next exhibit, 523?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a vehicle log for a TAM 75 truck registration number M-5329. This particular vehicle is assigned to the 6th Infantry Battalion at Petkovci. And the two individuals listed as drivers are listed as members of the 6th Infantry Battalion. On 15 July -- or starting on 14 July going through 15 July, three notations of 15 litres of fuel each. And then on the 14th, a final notation of 7 litres of fuel. And as I've discussed before, a TAM 75 is a medium-sized cargo truck. Going to page 2 of this particular document, looking at the activity on 15 July 1995, it reflects a number of trips -- I'll have to look at the original. I believe four trips. You'll see it listed here. And you will see notations between Petkovci and Brana, which is, to my understanding, the B/C/S word for dam. And it talks about other movement activity as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. But to be -- again, to be clear, this is not engineering equipment. This is --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. These are subordinate to the 6th Infantry Battalion. They are not engineering equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Prosecution Exhibit 524, another TAM 80 truck. Registration number M-5300. The two individuals, again listed as drivers with the 6th Battalion. And on 15 July 1995, six journeys back and forth between Petkovci, Brana, and Petkovci, a total of 48 kilometres driven.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go on to the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Going back to the military context of the situation, this is the 15 July 1995 regular combat report to the command of the Drina Corps from the command of the 1st Zvornik Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it is Exhibit 526.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And why have you chosen this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It discusses this paragraph 1 the larger enemy attack which is now occurring as of 0440 hours and it ended at approximately 0530 hours and the enemy is continuing to fire artillery weapons. And again the units that are being isolated for attack are the 4th, 6th and 7th Infantry Battalions. In this particular respect, knowing from the intercepts of Bosnian Muslim conversations, even those taken by the VRS that this was designated to be the area where they believed that the column was going to be coming out and attempting to break through the lines into BH territory, and, in fact, this is what occurred. So in this respect, forces of the 24th Infantry Division of BH 2 Corps began launching attacks along the front lines of the 4th, 6th, and 7th Battalions, in order to keep their front line forces engaged so they could not be used for combat against the column which was now approaching towards their rear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Unless there's anything else on this document in the military situation, we can go to the next document, which is 527, the ...

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: 527, this is the daily combat report of the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade for 15 July 1995, and we've discussed this document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So why do you bring it back?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only bring it back to highlight the issue in paragraph 2, that correlating to the duty officer workbook index and even the garrison log, the notation that a group of soldiers, approximately 80, has been sent from the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade zone to the Zvornik Infantry Brigade zone. And we see those notations in the various books. And just a piece that I use to confirm events as they're occurring in context.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Does this issue of reinforcements coming from Bratunac, does that become relevant in some analysis of an intercept on the 16th of July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it will.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. We'll hopefully get there soon. The next exhibit, 528, an interim combat report from the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an interim combat report from the command of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade to the command of the Drina Corps. It states in great detail the situation in the zone of the Zvornik Brigade, both the military situation and it also discusses the situation with respect to large numbers of prisoners distributed throughout schools in the brigade's area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I think this has been discussed, but can you just tell us what your interpretation is of that first sentence, "An additional burden for us is the large number of prisoners distributed throughout the schools in the brigade area, as well as obligations of security and restoration of the terrain."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given the military situation and the context when this report is drafted, in the late afternoon of 15 July 1995, this is the commander of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade, Colonel Pandurevic, telling the Drina Corps that the dual responsibilities of dealing with the issue of the column and dealing with the issue of the prisoners, of guarding the prisoners, and then burying the bodies afterwards is now to point where he cannot resource both operations. He indicates that if no one takes responsibility -- on this responsibility, "I will be forced to let them go." Now, as I've noted in my prior testimony, that is somewhat of an empty threat, given that the locations of where these prisoners are, it would be very unlikely that Colonel Pandurevic would just open the door and let thousands of Bosnian Muslims who are now presently located well behind his own front lines meander towards BiH territory at the time. But it does, in effect, reflect his frustration with the circumstances that his brigade is in, given these two tasks, and given the critical situation developing with the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: By the evening when it appears this -- well, can you give us an idea of when you think this report was sent or received.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looking at the original B/C/S version, you have the communications centre stamp indicating that it was sent at 1925 hours on 15 July 1995. And perhaps this will be more clear on the English language one where we were able to see on the original. I will also go back and note that again in this particular instance, recognising the signature of select individuals through my analysis of hundreds of their documents, this is a signature that I believe represents or is the signature of Colonel Vinko Pandurevic, the commander of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade. It is rather distinctive and it does lend itself to rather easy identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, by this time around 7 -- 1900 hours, where, as far as you know from your study, are prisoners still alive in the Zvornik Brigade area?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this particular time, the prisoners that were stored at the school in Orahovac are dead --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, getting in practice, try to ask my questions as specifically as you can. I just asked --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where they're alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- where they're alive.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. They are alive in the school in Kula, Pilica. Our information is that those executions don't occur until the 16th of July in the morning. They are alive in the dome of culture in Pilica. And there still remains an ongoing question as to the number that may be alive in the school at Rocevic. We have no documents or intercepts which would give any evidence as to when the prisoners were executed in that school. So from documents and evidence alone, I don't know. There have been individuals who have raised the issue with the investigation that the prisoners may have been executed in Rocevic on 15 July 1995. But I don't have documents which might confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the next exhibit is a patient history, so if we could not put that on the ELMO. Can you just tell us why you've chosen this patient history of this particular individual. It appears to be a Muslim individual. It's Exhibit 529. And this -- we have offered it under seal just because it is a medical record.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you refer, and again I won't put it on the ELMO, if you refer to page 25 of the English language translation of the duty officer workbook, you will note that individual's name referenced as having died at the Zvornik hospital. The individual in question is an individual who was known through the records under P529 to have been captured, wounded, treated at the Milici medical centre, transferred to the Zvornik medical centre, and subsequently died there. I only raise that issue as, again, one of the pieces that I can use to indicate that notations in the book are reflecting the actual context of events as we understand them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, it appears just about time for the break. And it looks very good for us being able to finish today or come very close, just for your information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much. You are very optimistic. Well, we'll break and we'll resume at 12.30

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, let's go to the next exhibit for 16 July. I believe it's Exhibit 250, an intercept at 1111 hours.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could you tell us who this is -- we now Colonel Ljubo Beara by this time. Can you remind us who you think Cerovic is at this time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cerovic is Colonel Cerovic, who is normally the assistant commander for morale, legal, and religious affairs of the Drina Corps and whom on 16 July 1995, I believe, is also functioning as the duty officer of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what do you think this conversation is about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the context the first thing he notes is an individual named Trkulja is here with him now. I was looking for you, in respect, looking for Beara. As I have indicated in my previous testimony, Colonel Trkulja is an officer of the Main Staff. He is a member of the operations department. And the context of the conversation is that they need to do triage on those and then, of course, he's interrupted and it also notes that he's got instructions from above.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what do you think this triage means?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to triage having to be done on the prisoners, I believe what we are looking at here is a euphemism for the prisoners need to be executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Unless there's anything else on this, we can go to the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Prosecution Exhibit 252.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And what is this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a 16 July series of intercepts at 1358 hours which take place between initially the Zlatar duty officer and the Palma duty officer. And the first part of the conversation it reflects that the Palma duty officer is relaying a message that 500 leaders of D2 fuel are needed for colonel or Lieutenant Colonel Popovic. It disconnects and then he's reconnected. And the next correspondent who's talking is Basevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who do you think Basevic is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular reference, Major Basevic is an individual who's identified as the chief of technical services of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And what do you think they're talking about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular instance, they're now discussing that Lieutenant Colonel Popovic is here at Palma. He knows that. And that 500 litres of D2 are urgently being asked for him or else the work he's doing will stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you think what the work -- well, first of all who do you think "he" is in that sentence?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe "he" in that sentence is Lieutenant Colonel Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what do you think the work is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The work that's occurring at that point in time in the zone of the Zvornik Brigade that Colonel Popovic would be involved in would be the movement of prisoners from the school in Pilica by bus to the Branjevo Military Farm where they're being executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you have some other materials to help back that up that we'll be getting to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that in concert with some of the other documents as well as the testimony of Mr. Erdemovic during the Krstic which reflects buses arriving filled with prisoners from the school in Pilica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And can you -- let's go into the second page of this. There's more talk about 2 tons arriving. It says, "Well then, get in touch with Rosevic." Do you know what means?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I have not been able to identify an individual with that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We know there's a place where there's a school. Have you been able to make any connection with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then it goes on: "Did you get Basevic?" And then P says: "Yes, I did. And who is that? Is it the duty officer?" Then C says: "The switchboard. And give me the operations duty officer. Is Major Golic there by chance?" Then: "Yes. Let me talk to him." Then P is: "Golic, pop just called me and told me to contact you. 500 litres of D2 have to be sent to him immediately, otherwise his work will stop." Again, Major Golic, who do you think that is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Golic is an intelligence officer with the command of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Then it goes on and they talk about: "Yeah, 500 litres, or else his work will stop. Go on right away. Bye." Then P says: "A bus loaded with oil is to go to Pilica village. That's it." Then X says: "500 litres." Now, this comment: "A bus loaded with oil is to go to Pilica," what do you think what means?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think in this respect what they're referring to is a -- not necessarily a bus but something that's towing a container with 500 litres of fuel with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Pilica village, can you just briefly describe the size of that village, as you know it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is that Pilica village is a very small village, literally built on a crossroads in the northern end of the Zvornik municipality. It's not a very populated village at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So it goes on: "No, it should go its fuel tank from the vehicle battalion." And X says: "So it's separate?" P says: "Yes, yes, it should be separate." And then says: "Struck through: Just need." Then P says: "There is, but Colonel Krsmanovic over at your place has to call here to the vehicle battalion." Now, can you remind us who P should be in this conversation.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: P should be the Palma duty officer in this conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And again, Lieutenant Colonel Krsmanovic, what do you think this comment about him means.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In context, Lieutenant Colonel Krsmanovic, as we've discussed, is the chief of transportation [Realtime transcript read in error "communication"] services for the Drina Corps. Because of the near or almost co-location of one of the logistics bases of the Drina Corps at Standard which has some assets there, Colonel Krsmanovic as the corps transportation officer has to call down and authorise the use of one of those vehicles to bring 500 litres of fuel up to Pilica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. McCloskey, can I make a clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: The transcript said about Colonel Krsmanovic, that he was the chief of communication. As I understood Mr. Butler, he said the chief of transportation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: We can correct that in the transcript, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And just, can you remind us how important fuel was for the VRS at this juncture in the war.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As perhaps best evidenced by the vehicle logs that we've seen in the last several exhibits, fuel was an extremely critical resource, and it was something that obviously due to a scarcity had a great deal of value on the black market. Consequently there was a significant effort by all military parties to make sure that the fuel was all properly accounted for and was used in the proper manner. Again, that's reflected by the -- from the very beginning that each vehicle has to account for how much fuel is in it on any given day, when it receives it, that orders have to be written to that effect. So it was obviously scarce to the army. And as a result of being somewhat scarce to the community in general, it was something that had a high degree of value associated with it. So theft and pilferage would not be uncommon. So that's why in this context the military takes the steps that it does to ensure that the fuel they do have is regulated to the best of its ability.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next exhibit then; it's 530. Tell us what it is, where the OTP got it, and then explain it.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was obtained by OTP during their search of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade or the headquarters of the former Infantry Brigade, Zvornik Infantry Brigade, in the beginning of 1998. This is the receipt issued by the military post 7469, which is the Zvornik Infantry Brigade, to Lieutenant Colonel Popovic for 500 litres of D2 diesel fuel on 16 July 1995. And it also notes that out of the 500 litres, 140 were returned. It's issued according to the order of Captain Sreten Milosevic, who is the assistant commander for rear services for the Zvornik Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what's the significance of this document for your analysis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the original, just for the ELMO. There are several levels of significance for me on this one. The first one, of course, is the one directly related to the intercept process. This document as a military document in the headquarters of the Zvornik Brigade is not a document that was public in any manner, and therefore, it's an excellent document which I use to corroborate the reliability with respect to parts of the intercept process where they're discussing the content of the conversation. Clearly when you're looking for something such as a deliberate deception, and you always have to be aware of that, the fact that there's no conceivable way by which the BiH 2 Corps intercept operators would have had access to these documents inside the building of their opposition, their wartime opposition, and then to be able after the fact be able to lash-up the intercept and the documents corroborates on one hand the authenticity of the material, and it also gives you an indication as to how reliable the pick-up was of the information in question. On a different level, this document also helps to confirm the analysis that I've offered previously with respect to the limits of the security officer with respect to his powers to obtain material and resources outside of his normal purview. In this particular instance, looking at the context of the intercept, Colonel Popovic is directing the Palma duty officer to call the -- to call the Zlatar duty officer to the headquarters of the Drina Corps in order to get approval for the dispersal of 500 litres of fuel. Obviously he was aware that to try and make an order of that on his own was not something he was authorised to do and that he would need the approval of the rear services department of the Drina Corps in order to effect that. So you see through the intercept and the document the manifestation of a proper command and staff process in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In fact, does the brigade rear services people get involved in this authorisation process as well?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And once, in fact, the approval is given - and I don't have an intercept which, in fact, indicates that it was given in that context - but certainly some form of approval was given to the assistant commander for rear services of the Zvornik Brigade which would allow for the dispersal of fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Exhibit 530 says in the English version: "Fuel is issued according to the order of Captain S. Milosevic," and then remark, "Out of 500 litres of D2, 140 litres were returned." So, again S. Milosevic --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is Captain Sreten Milosevic, the assistant commander for rear services of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just to clarify, down at the bottom there is a special service organ and it looks like M. Krstic. Do you know who that is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No -- I do know who it is. It is not General Krstic. In fact, it is an individual, I believe his name is Milorad Krstic who is a clerk in the special services and technical services organ who does accounting issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is there anything else you want to say about this document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to Exhibit 257, an intercept 16 July, 2116 hours, involving Popovic and others. Now, this particular intercept -- has part of your analysis of this intercept changed from your analysis of it during the Krstic case?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it has.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, let's go through it now and get your analysis as it currently is, and then I'll ask you some questions about how your analysis has changed and why. So let's begin with P, and who is that supposed -- who do you believe that to be, when it says P?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As indicated in the first line, you have a voice compromise, and Lieutenant Colonel Popovic is identifying himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then the next one, Rasic here, can I help you. Any idea who Rasic is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand that Colonel Obrenovic has identified an individual named Rasic as a security individual associated with the Drina Corps. And based on the material that I have, I'm not able to confirm that identity. So I'm just going to have to remain that I'm not sure who that person is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And Popovic says: "I was just up there." What do you think he's referring to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular context, particularly coupled with his comment in the next one "With the boss personally," I believe that he was up at the IKM of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade with Colonel Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is there new information you've received that assists that analysis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this overall context Colonel Obrenovic had indicated that the terminology "up" also refers to, with respect, from a lower terrain feature to a higher terrain feature. And that is a logical conclusion that could be drawn. And again as I try to be as conservative with these intercepts as possible, I believe that interpretation is a fair one, and I would adopt that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was there some sort of reference in the workbook that we've spoken to and we will get to later relating to Popovic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you just briefly, since we're at this conversation, relate to us what you recall about the workbook, and then we'll go on on the intercept.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Part of the genesis of this intercept will be that as the historical context indicates, the pressure on the Zvornik Brigade by the column during the morning and early afternoon hours of 16 July 1995 become so great that Colonel Pandurevic, on his own authority, essentially declares a battlefield truce and opens a hole for the column to pass unmolested into BiH territory. This directive on his part was not authorised by either the Drina Corps or the Main Staff or the president of the Republic. And as word that this event has occurred starts travelling through the military and civilian chains of information, you see a series of attempts by commanders at the Drina Corps and in a series of intercepts, that I don't believe I have in toto here, by the Main Staff to contact Colonel Pandurevic and to get an explanation from Colonel Pandurevic exactly what he's doing and what's going on. This conversation, in part, is based at the back end of that whole series of events, where Colonel Popovic is discussing that issue as well as other issues related to executions at Branjevo Farm, passing that information back to the Zlatar duty officer, and again noting in context he had originally asked to be connected with General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recall the notation in the workbook involving Popovic in this issue?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Again, can you just -- before we get to it, just tell us what that is. You don't need to go back to it. Just generally. We'll get to the specifics of it. Just to keep the context of this conversation.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It specifically notes in one of the items, it says: "Message from Zlatar that Lieutenant Colonel Popovic must go to Vinko Pandurevic in the field at 1640 hours."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So getting back to the conversation: "I was with the boss personally." Who do you think that is again?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that is Colonel Vinko Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And R says: "Yes." Popovic says: "Here where I am. You know where I am." Where do you think Popovic is when he's saying this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In respect to the fact that they know that their communications are liable to intercept, he does not want to say exactly where he is, so he is trying to talk around the subject. He is at the Palma headquarters of the Zvornik Brigade right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We know that Colonel Popovic is spending the day or has spent most of the day of 16 July 1995 in the zone of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade, and given the fact that he's talking on his communication node and given the fact that call is originating from Palma leads me to make the conclusion that he's at the headquarters of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Then R says: "I know." Popovic says: "Well, you got his interim report." What do you think Popovic is referring to with that, "got his interim report"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this respect, they're referring to an interim report published by the command of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade on 16 July 1995, and we will look at that document next. That is Prosecution Exhibit 531.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then R says: "All of it." And Popovic says: "It's all just like he wrote ... I was there on the spot and was convinced he had received some numbers." What do you think he means by that section of the statement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this respect, as indicated in a series of exhibits that will be discussed, based on the growing size and threat of the column, a large number of units are notified to send reinforcements into the zone of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade. One of the issues that occurs is that these reinforcements do not arrive in time, at least as far as Colonel Pandurevic is concerned, and that as a result of these reinforcements not arriving, he had to take the action to allow the column to pass. From the context of the Drina Corps and the other command, they knew that these reinforcements had been established, setting the context that even though Colonel Pandurevic had received adequate reinforcement, he still had let the column go. As we see in the historical context, that very issue will become a bone of contention between the Zvornik Infantry Brigade and the Drina Corps and the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So then it says: "Well, that's not even important ... I'll come there tomorrow, so tell the General I've ... I've finished the job." What do you think he means when he says: "I'll come there tomorrow"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he's informing them that he'll return to the headquarters of the Drina Corps on 17 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then what about -- what does this mean in your opinion: "So tell the General ... I've finished the job." What General? Do you have any idea who he's referring to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given the context of two officers of the Drina Corps discussing an issue, my conclusion is that the General in question is, in fact, General Krstic, the Drina Corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I've finished the job, what do you think he means by that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe in that respect, the job he's discussing as being finished is the execution of Bosnian Muslims at the Branjevo Military Farm and at the Pilica dome.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why couldn't that be the job he was assigned to go see what Pandurevic was up to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looking at that in context with, first of all, why he was in the zone of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade in the first place, and another sentence with respect to: Have you finished -- and I finished everything, I believe that in this context what we're discussing is his job which was to oversee the execution of the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So on 16 July at 2116 hours, what was the situation with the prisoners in the Zvornik Brigade zone?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the exception of our handful of survivors, all of the prisoners at all of the holding sites had already been executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Then it says: "Good." And Popovic says: "I'll come there tomorrow when I'm sure that that's all been taken care of, you know." What do you think he means by that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As other documents will lay out, future exhibits, we know that while the executions occurred on 16 July 1995, the actual process of burying the bodies did not begin until the morning of the 17th. I believe that is the thing that he wants to ensure is taken care of before he returns.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And R says: "Good." P says: "After I bring a transport from there." Do you know what that means?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't know what that means in context.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Then R says: "Right." Then Popovic says: "Well, in general there weren't any major problems, but up there there were horrible problems and that thing the commander sent, it was just the right thing." Now, this somewhat difficult sentence, can you make any sentence out of this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Breaking it down, the first sentence: "Well, in general there weren't any major problems." Given the context of all the things that have already been discussed and the issues with the column, I believe that in this respect he's talking about the mass executions, because there were two problem issues occurring in the Zvornik Brigade sector, one was of the issue of the column, one was the issue of mass executions. Certainly the historical context sets out very clearly that there were tremendous problems with the column. So in context, this is Colonel Popovic informing Rasic that there weren't any major problems with the execution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Then we get to this sentence: "But up there." What do you think he means by "up there"? That's another reference to up there.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this context, and this is where my opinion will be changing from how I previously viewed this, I will subscribe to Colonel Obrenovic's interpretation of up there as being up at the -- in the area of the battlefield, which would be towards IKM and towards the Baljkovica area where the brunt of the most significant fighting is taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So why are you changing your mind?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, in this context, and I've always tried to note as a component of my total analysis, if a document or an intercept was open to multiple interpretations, particularly in the issue between a criminal interpretation and a strictly military one, that as a matter of practice when it was, I would always default back to that military interpretation. That's as I professionally view it, a component of attempting to keep my analysis of the material as conservative as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And it goes on to say, "As we've said, but up there. There were horrible problems." And what do you think he's referring to when he says: "There were horrible problems"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this respect he's discussing the issue of the pitched battle between the column and the forces of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the next part: The thing the commander sent, it was just the right thing. What do you think that means?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is interesting phrase, given the historical context of what we know had occurred. As we'll discuss in the 16 July interim combat report from the Zvornik Brigade, Colonel Pandurevic is making it very clear that because the reinforcements did not arrive in time, that is why he was forced to open up the hole and let the column go through. And in this context, Colonel Popovic is saying that the thing that the commander sent is just the right thing. So I'm not sure whether they're all talking about the same thing in this respect, because at least from Colonel Obrenovic's -- I'm sorry, Colonel Pandurevic's point of view, it arrived too late. It wasn't the right thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, then, let me take you briefly back, and if you could provide us a -- just a very brief summary of what will be part of the record of this case and was already part of the Krstic case, that is some of the high points of Mr. Erdemovic and I want to keep very particular issues on this. What in particular did Mr. Obrenovic say was the problem that his unit was dealing with in the murder of some 1.000 Muslim prisoners on the 16th of July at the Branjevo Farm?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The specific problem that his unit or the unit that he was a member of at that time, which consisted of six people, I believe, was that first of all there were many people coming to be executed. Secondly, there were so few of them. And third, I believe Mr. Erdemovic details that very early in the morning members of that six-person squad started drinking, and that very quickly as a component of that, while some members of the squad were very enthusiastic about conducting the executions, other members of that squad were not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So from what Mr. Erdemovic said, did his unit get any assistance with their problem at some point that day at Branjevo Farm?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In his testimony, Mr. Erdemovic notes that in the early afternoon hours of 16 July 1995, a group of soldiers from Bratunac arrives and assists in the execution process.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Going back, did you have a chance to look over your Krstic testimony on the subject?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in your Krstic testimony, did you make a mistake in relating Mr. Erdemovic's information?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did and I recognised that when I reviewed my transcript testimony approximately a week ago on that. And I had misspoke, and one of the things I asked for was, as soon as I recognised what I had said, that the tape be checked, because attributed to me is the observation that Erdemovic had said, "Men from the Bratunac Brigade." And I would like to go on record as saying that from the very beginning of my association with this case, I have always known that Erdemovic has always said that it was men or soldiers from Bratunac. He has never indicated that they were men from the Bratunac Brigade, and that is a fact that I know. And that is why I asked for a clarification as to whether that was actually something I had said. If I did say it, I did misspeak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, then -- with that factual backdrop in mind, let me go back. "But up there, there were horrible problems, and the thing the commander sent, it was just the right thing." Did you have what Mr. Erdemovic said in mind when you made your analysis on this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's keep going. R says: "Good. " P says: "Just the thing. Horrible. It was horrible." And then Rasic says: "Listen, Vujadin." Does that clear up any problems with who Lieutenant Colonel Popovic might have been?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Popovic says: "What." R says: "Tell me. Did anything arrive there now from Vidoje Blagojevic." So what -- Vidoje Blagojevic, who is that in this context in your view?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this context, that is the commander of the Bratunac -- of the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what do you think Rasic is asking when he's asking: "Tell me, did anything arrive there now from Vidoje Blagojevic"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the context of the other information which we'll get to, and it is noted various units were directed to send additional troops to the zone of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade. And in this respect, Rasic is asking whether or not those troops that had been sent or that were supposed to have been sent from Bratunac, whether they have arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Popovic -- well, he clears up that issue and says: "Yes, you mean manpower?" Rasic says: "Yes, yes. Did anything arrive? Something was supposed to arrive." Then Popovic says in another interesting comment: "Yes, it arrived ... It's up there." What do you think in the context of this whole thing he's referring to now?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this respect, he's referring to his awareness that a group of soldiers from Bratunac had finally arrived and being sent up there, they were sent in the direction of the forward command post or the Baljkovica area of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Then it goes on: "It's up there, but it didn't arrive on time and it wasn't brought in on time." What do you think that means?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In effect he's reiterating that the reinforcements arrived late.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And he says: "And the others who arrived." Do you know these others are that he may be referring to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are a number of possibilities. As we'll see in a later intercept, there were reinforcements arriving from Dobos, which is the telephonic code name for the headquarters at Vlasenica. There were supposed to be some reinforcements from the Milici brigade, and there were supposed to be reinforcements arriving from a unit of the 16th Krajina Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about Erdemovic's guys from Bratunac? Would you include them as a possibility in here?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Then it goes on: "But they were late, so they weren't brought in on time. And that's why the commander who was here had problems." Now, what do you think he means by, "And that's why the commander who was here had problems"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the broader interpretation, the commander here would be Colonel Pandurevic. And they're talking about, in the larger context, the issue of the fact that since the reinforcements did not arrive on time, the commander, Colonel Pandurevic, had the problems and was forced to open up a hole for the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So in that sense, if the people who arrived late were the reason that Pandurevic had problems, would that be consistent with Erdemovic's guys from Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would generally not be consistent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Then we get to the next question, and it says: "When exactly did Blagojevic's men arrive?" He says: "[Expletive] I don't know exactly. Now I can't." And they go back and forth a bit and Rasic asks, sounds like the duty officer: "When did Blagojevic's men arrive?" The duty officer says: "From Badem" -- and they end it with: "I'll call you back." Now, do you have an intercept that you now incorporate into your analysis of this last part that you were not aware of at the Krstic trial?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But before we get to it, can you tell me, initially what was your view on this issue related to the arrival of Blagojevic's men?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That view initially migrated over several years with respect to my analysis of that situation. Based on Mr. Erdemovic's statements and testimony at his own trial, as well as the documents that we received from the Bratunac Brigade, my initial conclusion was that these people were probably from the Bratunac Brigade. As a following series of that investigation continued, the investigation was able to identify an individual who was known to be a member of the Panteri unit from the East Bosnia Corps and who was in Bratunac on 13 July 1995, and I believe that has been brought to this Court's attention. When that part of the information became available and I was able to analyse it and synthesise it, in the context of the Krstic trial, I testified to that effect during the rebuttal case of the Prosecution, where I noted that my position on that had changed based on new information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And is there even some more information that has assisted that analysis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly with respect to the physical presence of the individual from the Panteri unit, as part of the OTP's ongoing investigation, they were able to discover references to him being in Zvornik at the medical centre on that day, having treatment for an injury. So I believe that as the investigation has continued, we've been able to substantially corroborate the fact that that individual, and perhaps members of that unit, were in the Zvornik area and will have been at Branjevo Military Farm on 16 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just for the record, that is protected witness P188.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next intercept on the same issue, Exhibit 258?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a synopsis of an intercepted conversation with respect to Colonel Cerovic and the duty officer. As I had indicated, Colonel Cerovic on 16 July 1995 is the duty officer at the headquarters of the Drina Corps. And it reflects in a general roll-up when reinforcements arrived in the zone of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade. And it notes that a number had arrived from Badem, and I believe it's actually readable more on the handwritten version of this, but it's at 2100 hours or roughly 2130 hours, men from -- or 30 men from Dobos, which is Vlasenica, at 1715 hours and 20 men from Banja Luka -- I'm sorry -- it's 30 men from Badem, 20 men from Dobos at 1715, and 100 men from Banja Luka. And that corresponds to our knowledge of the size and the locations of where reinforcements from those units were arriving in the zone of the Zvornik Brigade on 16 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So going back to Mr. Erdemovic's men from Bratunac, what time did they arrive to the Branjevo Farm?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the testimony of the Krstic case of Mr. Obrenovic, they had arrived approximately midday, or noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, going back to Witness P188 who testified that he was in Bratunac on the morning of the 16th with others from his unit in a -- and were transported in, I think, a small TAM 110 vehicle. Now, if he and others ended up at the Branjevo Farm at 1.00 p.m., as Erdemovic says, who were the -- the sort of military options of where and who he would have received -- or his unit would have received instructions from?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps the most instructive model to use in this instance is the chain of events which Drazen Erdemovic says occurred by which his unit was instructed to begin that task or go to those various locations. In his testimony, and I don't want to paraphrase it, he does indicate that it was not a direct route, and that they were instructed by one of their superior officers to report to the headquarters of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade, Standard, and that there they would be met by another officer who would then take them further down the line. And as Erdemovic notes, they did go to the headquarters of the Zvornik Brigade, they were met by another officer, and they were taken to the location which we know is the Branjevo Military Farm where they were instructed what their mission was and what they were expected to do. Logically setting that to the next group of individuals, somebody would have had to have contact these individuals in the Bratunac area and instructed them to report to the Zvornik Infantry Brigade headquarters at Standard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Who were the ranking officers that you know of were in Bratunac on the morning of the 16th of July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a number of ranking officers. It is my understanding that Colonel Radoslav Jankovic of the Main Staff was still in Bratunac on 16 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where was he working out of?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would have working out of the headquarters of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who else?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Blagojevic would have, of course, been there. Captain First Class Momir Nikolic, the security officer. Lieutenant Micic would have been there as an operations officer. Major Trisic, the assistant commander for rear services, would have been there. So generally speaking, the whole suite of officers from the Bratunac Brigade who would normally be expected to be there would be there, the exception, of course, being the chief of staff who was deployed out of area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And does this reflect, as far as you know, the investigation's knowledge on that particular subject?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that is where we are to date with that particular subject, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go on to the next exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We may not make it, Your Honour, you may have been right. But we're going to be very close.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I believe it's 531, and this is 16 July interim combat report that you have earlier made reference to regarding that intercept that makes reference to a report. Is that right, Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And again just another example of how a piece of information that would not logically be in the possession of the ABiH references to it turn up in the intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't think we need to go into the detailed information in this report, but is this roughly consistent with some of the references that Popovic was making about numbers in that previous intercept?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And in that respect, paragraph 3 is where Colonel Pandurevic reflects the fact that under the circumstances, I have decided in view of the situation to open a corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So that's what you refer to when you say he made that decision without authorisation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why do you think he made such a drastic -- I won't say -- keep the adjectives out. Why did he make such a decision without authorisation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he makes that quite clear in paragraph 3, where he notes the inability of his own forces to hold out because portions of them have been surrounded. That the brigade has been abandoned, his perspective, to deal with the Srebrenica Turks as best they can, coupled with the absolute determination of the column to save their own -- to at least save some of their own lives, regardless of losses. So I think it's a reflection with respect to Colonel Pandurevic, it's a decision that as far as he was concerned is inevitable under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next exhibit, it's 532. It's the regular combat report that would have come before the interim. Do we need to -- is there something in there that you want to point out?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. Just to continue the general historical context is why I offered this up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So nothing in particular?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. What's the next exhibit along those lines?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is 533, I believe.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. This is the daily combat of the Drina Corps for that same day, reflecting the general situation in the zone, and specific to the Zvornik Brigade. It discusses the situation in the Zvornik Brigade with detached units blocking these areas. Now, in this respect, given the reporting situation when this report is being drafted at 1937 hours or being sent by 1937 hours, there's still not a full awareness on the point of the Drina Corps just exactly what Colonel Pandurevic has done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's go back -- I think we're now going back to the engineering order book for 16 July, which is Exhibit 535?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: On 16 July, just the notations on items 2 and 3 that work is still continuing, at least in the early morning as far as their understanding is, of engineering work at Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And let's go to -- do you have some vehicle logs on that point, Exhibit 536?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: And on this particular day, this is the Torpedo Excavator from Birac Holding, 60 litres of fuel. However, on this day, it reflects that the activity by this particular piece of equipment has now shifted from Orahovac, and they are now digging trenches at Kozluk, which is the burial location for those executed from the school at Rocevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next exhibit, 537, a 17 July engineering order book.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular context, bullets points 2 and 3 note the work of BGH-700 at Branjevo and the work of ULT-220 at Branjevo. And it notes on task 5 that a BGH-700 is to be transported to Branjevo by a flatbed truck. So in this instance while they have the tasks actually out of proper order, it notes the fact that the BGH-700 is going be brought to Branjevo and it will be employed at Branjevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What's happening Branjevo then?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: 17 July 1995, at Branjevo military farm, engineer equipment of the Zvornik Brigade is engaged in burying the bodies from the executions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you briefly explain your comment"at Branjevo military farm"? How do you know that's true?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have documents in this part of the investigation, area known as Branjevo farm is in fact a military farm that is part of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade and it's under the custody of the 1st Infantry Battalion. There are a series of documents which are in my narrative which tie that all in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's then go to the Exhibit 260, it's an intercept and what date should this be?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This intercept is 17 July 1995 at 0615 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And briefly -- well, who do you think Captain Trbic is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain Trbic is a security officer for the Zvornik Infantry Brigade. I also believe that Captain Trbic was performing the duty officer function of the Zvornik Brigade from the morning of 16 July trough the morning of 17 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Going down this intercept where General Krstic is alleged to have said: Okay. Have you killed the Turks up there? And Trbic says: Well, I guess you got the report. What more can I tell you? What do you think Krstic is talking about there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this respect, I believe that General Krstic is discussing the issues with the column and that the report in question is either the regular or the interim combat report by the Zvornik Brigade which discusses that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And after that, General Krstic speaks with Vinko Pandurevic later on. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir. And on page 2 of the English language --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: They're just discussing the military situation at the time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. What's the next exhibit?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Prosecution Exhibit 358 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry, apparently that is a mistake. It is actually 538. We need to -- want to make that change.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: And it's for a Mercedes 2626 vehicle, registration number M-5195. Its task on 17 July was noted from Base, Standard, Branjevo, and then return to Base, and its task consisted of the transport of the 700 loader.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know if Milan Milovanovic, the person listed as the driver/user, is part of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember offhand at this time. That is something that we can, of course, check.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Anything else from this document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Other than it's consistent with the engineer logbook showing what the tasks were for the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you have the engineering roster in front of you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would actually be easier if I looked in this binder. Okay. Here's my copy, so I can ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's all right, Mr. Butler, we'll see if we can --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here it is. Down at the bottom, number 6, Milan Milovanovic listed as a driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: From the engineering company?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: For July of 1995, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And what's our next exhibit?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is -- just quickly back to Exhibit 518, reflecting that on 17 July, 100 litres of D2 went into the BGH-700.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And then the next document.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is Exhibit 522, construction machine owned by Birac Holding, reflecting the activity of 17 July, digging trenches in Branjevo and 8.5 hours driven.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And again, that's the exhibit where there's a mistake, an old 220 is a loader, not a backhoe excavator. All right. And if we could go to --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exhibit 237.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go to 237. Tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a conversation between two correspondents with respect to the identification of an individual who was captured from the column, who is reportedly Naser Oric's chief signalman. And in the context for me why this intercept is of value is in respect that we do know of this individual and that he did, in fact, survive the war. And it also identifies that on 17 July 1995, that the two correspondents here that -- know that Colonel Stankovic was in Zvornik today. Colonel Stankovic is an officer from the intelligence directorate of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I just want to make sure we have that exhibit number correct. This intercept should be P273. And what's the next exhibit?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It will be Prosecution Exhibit 539, which the Trial Chamber has seen before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I believe you discussed those two -- paragraphs 1 and 2 at that time.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: So in respect, just the -- again, a part of the confirmation piece that under the circumstances the ABiH intercept people would not have known about the presence of Milorad Stankovic in the zone at that time, to be corroborated by another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Next exhibit, I believe, is 540.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the 18 July 1995 interim combat report from the command of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade.
